title: Metric system
wiki_lead:
A system of measurement is a frame in which physical qualities (such as length, weight, temperature, etc.) can be quantified with numbers. Among many systems of measurement, the metric system refers to ones that standardise a set of base units and a nomenclature describing relatively large and small quantities using decimal-based multiplicative unit prefixes (such as kilo and milli). The International System of Units (SI) is a good example, and there are other widely accepted systems (less popular than SI) mainly used in specific fields, such as the Gaussian units for electromagnetism.
Though rules governing the metric system have changed over time, the modern definition in the International System of Units prescribes the metric prefixes and seven base units: metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol), and candela (cd).
An SI derived unit is a named combination of base units, such as the hertz (cycles per second), newton (kg⋅m/s2), and tesla (1 kg⋅s−2⋅A−1). In the case of degrees Celsius (°C), it is a shifted scale derived from the kelvin (273.15 K is equal to 0 °C while 1 K interval is same to the 1 °C interval).
The SI system derives from the older metre-kilogram-second (MKS) system of units, though the definitions of the base units have evolved over time. Today, all base units are defined by physical constants – not by prototypes in the form of physical objects, as they were in the past.
Other metric system variants include the centimetre–gram–second system of units, the metre–tonne–second system of units, and the gravitational metric system. Each has unaffiliated metric units, and some of these systems are still used in limited contexts. Particular non-SI units such as the litre remain widely used.

Adoption

The SI system has been adopted as the official system of weights and measures in almost all countries of the world.
A notable outlier is the United States (US). Although it uses the system in some contexts, the US has resisted full adoption, and continues to use different measurement systems.
Adopting the metric system is known as metrication.


Multiplicative prefixes

In the SI system and generally in older metric systems, multiples and fractions of a unit can be described via a prefix on a unit name that implies a decimal (base-10), multiplicative factor.

Base units
The decimalised system is based on the metre, which had been introduced in France in the 1790s. The historical development of these systems culminated in the definition of the International System of Units (SI) in the mid-20th century, under the oversight of an international standards body.
The historical evolution of metric systems has resulted in the recognition of several principles. A set of independent dimensions of nature is selected, in terms of which all natural quantities can be expressed, called base quantities. For each of these dimensions, a representative quantity is defined as a base unit of measure. The definition of base units has increasingly been realised in terms of fundamental natural phenomena, in preference to copies of physical artefacts. A unit derived from the base units is used for expressing quantities of dimensions that can be derived from the base dimensions of the system—e.g., the square metre is the derived unit for area, which is derived from length. These derived units are coherent, which means that they involve only products of powers of the base units, without any further factors. For any given quantity whose unit has a name and symbol, an extended set of smaller and larger units is defined that are related by factors of powers of ten. grok_lead: The metric system is a coherent, decimal-based framework of measurement units developed in France during the late 18th century to supplant inconsistent local standards with a universal system grounded in empirical properties of the Earth and water. Its foundational unitsâthe metre for length, defined as one ten-millionth of the meridian quadrant from pole to equator, and the kilogram for mass, equivalent to one cubic decimetre of water at its densestâembodied Enlightenment principles of rationality and invariance. Evolving through international treaties like the 1875 Metre Convention, it culminated in the 1960 establishment of the International System of Units (SI), refined in 2019 to define all seven base units (second, metre, kilogram, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela) via fixed physical constants, ensuring reproducibility independent of artifacts or prototypes. This structure yields derived units without scaling factorsâsuch as the joule for energy directly from kilogram, metre, and secondâfacilitating precise calculations in science, engineering, and trade across its near-global adoption. Despite these empirical advantages in coherence and decimal scalability, which minimize conversion errors empirically observed in metric-dominant economies, adoption controversies linger in holdout nations like the United States, where customary units persist amid debates over transition costs, cultural inertia, and sector-specific practicalities like aviation or construction.
